title: Cancer mortality decline and access to cancer drugs
asked: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked what policy decisions or healthcare investments most explain the 21% fall in cancer mortality since 2012 despite rising diagnoses, and how the benefits have reached lower-income and less health-literate Singaporeans equally.
response: Ms Rahayu Mahzam said advances in healthcare have led to earlier detection and better treatment, lowering cancer mortality and benefiting all patients, especially with universal access. She said more work is needed on prevention, including modifying risk factors, encouraging vaccinations and early screening. On the Cancer Drug List, she said treatments are assessed for clinical and cost effectiveness and clinical needs, thresholds are not published to protect negotiating leverage, and lower-income patients get higher means-tested subsidies. She cited early results of about 30% average price reductions, and 60% for some treatments, while saying higher-income individuals can still buy expensive insurance covering all drugs.

key_points.quote: more work needs to be done especially in cancer prevention to modify risk factors such as smoking, unhealthy diet, lack of physical activity and alcohol consumption

key_points.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam

key_points.quote: We do not publish the thresholds as this will have impact on our negotiating leverage with the industry

key_points.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
key_points.quote: Those from the lower-income groups would already get a higher means-tested subsidy

key_points.quote: we have seen a reduction in the price by about 30% on average and for some treatments, 60%

key_points.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
key_points.quote: There is nothing stopping the higher-income individuals from loading themselves with expensive insurance that actually covers all drugs

key_points.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
